items.prompt: What is a seam in this unit?
choices: A comment listing what a function relies on
A point where a dependency can be swapped
A place where two files get merged
items.explanation: A seam is where a dependency arrives from outside, so a test can substitute something else.

items.prompt: Why does a function that reads the real clock inside its body resist testing?
choices: Clocks run slower than any test runner does
Time values cannot be compared at all
The test cannot change what the clock says
items.explanation: With no way to hand in a different clock, the result depends on when the test runs.

items.prompt: A function is handed its clock as a parameter. What does that give you?
choices: A seam where a test can supply its own clock
A speed boost for every later call it runs
Protection against every kind of wrong answer
items.explanation: A parameter is the simplest seam: the caller decides which clock is used.

items.prompt: Where does a seam usually come from?
choices: Adding more comments above the function
Running the test twice and comparing results
Passing it in instead of grabbing it inside
items.explanation: Seams are created by changing where the dependency is obtained.

items.prompt: A test passes in March and fails in December with no code change. Likely cause?
choices: The function reads the real date and the test never set it
The test file grew longer over the months since it was written
The function ran out of memory in the colder months
items.explanation: A hidden dependence on the real date makes results change as the calendar moves.

items.prompt: Is a function that calls a database always untestable?
choices: Yes, databases can never be replaced in a test
No; a stand-in can replace it once a seam exists
Only if the database is written in another language
items.explanation: Testability depends on the seam, not on the kind of dependency.

items.prompt: Which function has no seam for time?
choices: One that calls the real clock inside its own body
One that is handed a clock by its caller
One that takes a source of random numbers as input
items.explanation: Calling the clock inside leaves nothing for a test to replace.

items.prompt: In the opening story, what changed between November and January?
choices: The trial end date written into the test
Only the real date, which it reads itself
The code inside the function body itself
items.explanation: Nothing in the code or test changed; the clock the function reads moved on.

items.prompt: A store-hours test passes when run at 2 pm but fails in an overnight run at 2 am. Neither the test nor the function changed. Best diagnosis?
choices: The overnight machine has a slower processor, so timing assertions in the test fail
The function needs more comments about the opening hours it checks against
It reads the real clock inside its body, so the result depends on run time
The test needs to run twice in a row before its result can be trusted
items.explanation: Same code, different results by time of day means the real clock is an uncontrolled input. A seam would let the test fix the time.
items.reference:
Where the dependency is obtained
no seam: the function reads the real clock in its own body, so the result depends on when it runs
seam: the clock arrives as a parameter, so a test hands in any clock it likes
the dependency is the same in both; only where it is obtained differs
Why: testability is decided by where a dependency comes from, not by what it is.
items.learnMore:
Seams

A seam is a point where a dependency arrives from outside instead of being grabbed inside. Time, randomness, networks and databases are all fine to depend on once they come in through a seam.

Common mistake

Concluding that a function is untestable because it uses time or a database. The missing piece is almost always the seam.
items.reflection: Think of something you cannot check reliably because it depends on a moment you do not control. What would you need to be able to set yourself?

items.prompt: pickWinner(entries) calls the real random generator inside its body. Which change creates a seam?
choices: Take a function that supplies the number, defaulting to the real generator
Call the real generator twice and use the average of both numbers, to smooth results
Move the call to the top of the function so it runs before anything else
Rename the function so its name states that the outcome is random
items.explanation: The seam is the new parameter; the default keeps production the same, and a test can pass a function returning a fixed number.

choices: One that returns the sum of the two numbers it is given

One that is handed a clock and reports whether that clock's date is a weekend

items.prompt: A clock that always returns 15 June 2026 is which kind of double?
choices: A fake
A spy
A stub
items.explanation: It returns one canned value with no logic and no memory of calls.

items.prompt: What does a stub keep track of?
choices: Every call, so the test can read them later
Nothing; it hands back canned values
A working copy of the data it stands in for
items.explanation: A stub has no state and no real logic.

items.prompt: What makes a fake a fake?
choices: It really works, in a simpler form
It always hands back the same fixed value
It records calls for the test to read
items.explanation: A fake has genuine behavior, such as actually storing what it is given.

items.prompt: An in-memory list standing in for a database is a…
choices: Stub
Spy
Fake
items.explanation: It behaves like a store, just without real infrastructure.

items.prompt: Which can store a refund and give it back later?
choices: A stub returning success
A fake in-memory gateway
A stub clock
items.explanation: Only a double with working state can hand back what it was given.

items.prompt: You need one fixed answer, once. What is enough?
choices: A fake with full storage
A strict mock
A stub
items.explanation: Choose the cheapest double that answers the question.

items.prompt: What does a fake cost compared with a stub?
choices: More code to build and keep correct
It cannot be used in tests
It has to be run against live production data
items.explanation: Realism has a build and maintenance price.

items.prompt: Both return data when called. What separates them?
choices: A stub always runs slower than a fake does, in every case
A fake never returns any data when called
A fake keeps working state; a stub returns canned values
items.explanation: State and real logic are what a fake has and a stub lacks.

items.prompt: A test saves two refunds, then asks the double for the list of refunds saved so far. Which double can answer correctly?
choices: A stub, because a canned value can be chosen to match whatever was saved
A spy, because the code under test reads back what the spy recorded
A strict mock, because it is told the saved values before the code runs
A fake, because its answers come from state built by earlier calls
items.explanation: Only a double with working state returns a list that reflects the saves. A stub's value is fixed in advance.
items.reference:
Canned versus working
stub: returns a fixed value, keeps no state, no real logic
fake: a simplified but genuinely working version, keeps state across calls
stub fits: force one situation
fake fits: a flow where later calls depend on earlier ones
Why: pick the cheapest double that still answers the question; a fake costs code and only proves fake-like behavior.
items.learnMore:
Stub versus fake

A stub is chosen to produce one situation. A fake lets a multi-step flow run for real against a small in-memory copy. The fake's gaps (limits, ordering, failures) are invisible to tests that only use it.

Common mistake

Building a full fake when the test needed one canned answer, or trusting a fake as proof the real dependency behaves the same.
items.reflection: Think of a practice run you do before the real thing. Which differences from the real thing might the practice run hide from you?

items.prompt: A test passes against an in-memory fake store, but the real database rejects duplicate refund ids that the fake accepts. What does this show?
choices: The fake was a stub in disguise, since it returned data without real logic
A fake only proves behavior against fake-like conditions; gaps can hide bugs
Fakes should never hold state, since state makes them behave unlike any real database
The real database must be wrong, since the test passed on the fake first
items.explanation: A fake is a simplification. A few tests against the real dependency catch what the fake leaves out.

A fake with full balance storage and update rules
A spy that records the balance requests for later review
A strict mock with the whole call sequence pre-programmed

items.prompt: A feature saves a note and then lists all notes. The test adds three notes and checks the list shows three. Which double stands in for the store?
choices: A stub returning a list of three notes, which would pass even if nothing were saved
A spy recording the save calls, which cannot hand the notes back to the code
A fake in-memory store, since the list must reflect what was really saved
A stub clock set to the day the notes were saved, which cannot hold notes
items.explanation: A stub returning three notes makes the test pass no matter what the code does. A fake makes the saving matter.

items.prompt: What does a spy record?
choices: How it was called: arguments and count
The return values of every other function
How long each test took to finish
items.explanation: A spy keeps a log of the calls it received.

items.prompt: When does a spy's check happen?
choices: Before the code runs, inside the spy itself
After the call, in the test's own code
Never; spies only return values
items.explanation: The test reads the recording afterward and asserts on it.

items.prompt: When does a strict mock check?
choices: During the call, failing itself on a mismatch
Only after all tests have finished
Never; it only ever returns canned values, no checks
items.explanation: A strict mock is given its expectations first and enforces them live.

items.prompt: Who does the asserting with a spy?
choices: The spy itself, as the call happens
The test, reading the recording
The production code under test
items.explanation: A spy is a passive recorder; the test judges.

items.prompt: A double that only records calls for later is, in precise terms, a…
choices: Stub
Fake
Spy
items.explanation: Many tools call it a mock, but recording for later inspection is a spy.

items.prompt: Which question does a spy answer?
choices: What happens if the dependency returns X?
Did my code call the dependency correctly?
Does the code work against a simplified working copy?
items.explanation: Interaction checks are what spies are for.

items.prompt: A test checks that refund was requested once, with ch_1. Which double fits?
choices: A spy
A stub
A fake
items.explanation: The call itself is the thing being verified, so it must be recorded.

items.prompt: A test only checks a return value for a fixed input. Is a spy needed?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, to count the calls
No; a stub is enough
items.explanation: If the call details are not the point, recording them only adds brittleness.

items.prompt: In test A the gateway double is told 'expect one refund of ch_1' before the code runs and fails itself on a second call. In test B the test reads the recorded calls after the run. Which is which?
choices: A uses a spy; B uses a strict mock
A uses a stub; B uses a fake
A uses a strict mock; B uses a spy
Both use spies, since both end in a check on calls
items.explanation: Checking live against pre-set expectations is a strict mock. Reading a recording afterward is a spy.
items.reference:
When the call is checked
stub: never checks calls, only returns a value
spy: records calls; the test asserts afterward
strict mock: told its expectations first; fails itself during the call
Why: use a spy or mock only when the fact of the call is what must be verified; otherwise a stub keeps the test free of internal details.
items.learnMore:
Spy versus mock

Both answer whether the code called its dependency correctly. A spy leaves the judging to the test after the run. A strict mock judges live and points at the exact call that broke its expectation. Many tools call a recorder a mock; by the precise terms it is a spy.

Common mistake

Asserting on every call detail by habit, which makes tests fail on harmless refactors.
items.reflection: Think of a check you do after a task versus a rule enforced while it happens. Which one catches problems earlier, and which is less annoying?

items.prompt: Which requirement truly needs a spy or mock rather than a stub?
choices: The job must never request one refund twice, and the result would not show it
The job must return the refunded user ids for a fixed set of users, in order, each time
The job must treat a trial as expired when the stub clock says 15 June
The job must return an empty list when no trial has expired
items.explanation: Only a double that sees the calls can show a duplicate request. The other checks are visible in the return value.

items.prompt: A team asserts the exact order and count of every helper call in each test. A harmless refactor reorders two internal calls and many tests fail. What went wrong?
choices: Spies cannot record order reliably, so the failures are false alarms from the spy
The refactor should have been blocked, since call order is public behavior of every function
The tests needed more stubs to cover the reordered calls
The tests encode how the code works inside rather than what it must achieve
items.explanation: Asserting on internals ties tests to the current implementation, so harmless changes break them.

choices: A strict mock, since its name says mock
A spy, since the test checks the recording after the call
A fake, since it replaces a real function with a working one
A stub, since it replaces the real function in the test
items.explanation: What decides the term is when and by whom the check happens, not the name a tool chooses.

items.prompt: In isTrialExpired(user, clock = real clock), what does the default do?
choices: Makes every test run more slowly
Production callers need no change
Forces every caller to pass a clock
items.explanation: The default hides the seam from callers that do not need it.

items.prompt: Why must the refund job forward its clock to the trial check?
choices: To make the code a bit shorter
Because a clock cannot be used twice
Otherwise the real clock comes back
items.explanation: An inner call with no argument silently uses the real clock.

items.prompt: A job takes a clock but does not pass it to the trial check. The stub clock is…
choices: Ignored; the check uses the real clock
Used by every inner call as expected
Replaced by a second stub automatically
items.explanation: The stub never reaches the place that reads time.

items.prompt: What is the risk of a required clock parameter with no default?
choices: Tests can no longer pass in a clock
The clock turns into a spy
Every existing caller must change
items.explanation: A default keeps the seam invisible to existing callers.

items.prompt: Stub clock is 14 days after a trial's end date. Is the trial expired?
choices: Yes, the clock is past the end date
No, the clock is earlier than the end date
It depends on the real date today
items.explanation: The check is clock greater than end date, and 14 days after is greater.

items.prompt: Stub clock is 16 days before a trial's end date. Is it expired?
choices: Yes, the clock is later than the end date
No, the clock is before the end date
It depends on the real date today
items.explanation: 16 days before the end means the trial is still running.

items.prompt: How many seams does the refund job have?
choices: Two: the clock and the gateway
One: only the payment gateway, nothing else
Zero: both are read inside the body
items.explanation: Both arrive as parameters.

items.prompt: Should every dependency get a seam?
choices: Yes, every one of them, always
No; only where control is missing
Only the system clock, never others
items.explanation: A seam is for dependencies that make deterministic testing hard.

items.prompt: The refund job accepts a clock but calls isTrialExpired(user) without it. The test passes a stub clock fixed at 15 June. When can the test fail?
choices: Only on 15 June, when the real and stub clocks happen to disagree
Never, because the stub clock was supplied to the job and so is always used
Only on days when the gateway double responds slowly
On days set by the real date, since the real clock decides who expired
items.explanation: The stub never reaches the check, so the default real clock is back in the chain.
items.reference:
Threading a seam
default clock: production callers need no change
test passes a stub clock to the outer function
the outer function must forward it to every inner call
a call that forgets to forward brings the real clock back
Why: a seam only removes the real dependency for the whole chain if every caller on the way down passes it along.
items.learnMore:
Seams down a call chain

The default parameter keeps production unchanged, but it also means an inner call with no argument quietly uses the real thing. Forwarding is what keeps the whole chain deterministic.

Common mistake

Adding the seam to the inner function and forgetting the function that calls it.
items.reflection: Think of an instruction that passes through several people. At which hand-off could it silently be replaced by a default?

items.prompt: Why is a default of the real clock preferable to a required clock parameter?
choices: Tests no longer need a stub, because the default is fixed at one date
Existing callers keep working unchanged, and tests can still pass a stub
The default guarantees every inner function receives the same clock
Required parameters are not allowed once a function has several callers
items.explanation: The default keeps the seam invisible in production while leaving it open for tests.

items.prompt: Implement `makeStubClock(ms)`: it returns a function that always returns `ms`.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const c = makeStubClock(9); c(); return c(); })()).toBe(9)

items.explanation: A stub clock keeps nothing and does nothing: it returns the value it was given.

items.prompt: Implement `isExpired(trialEndsAt, clock)`: true when `clock()` is greater than `trialEndsAt`.
items.explanation: The clock is a parameter, so the test controls it. At exactly the end the trial has not yet expired.

items.prompt: Implement `makeStubGateway()`: an object whose `refund(chargeId)` always returns `{ success: true }`.
items.explanation: A stub answers the same way every time and remembers nothing.

items.prompt: Implement `makeLog()`: an object with a `calls` array and a `refund(chargeId)` method that pushes `chargeId` onto `calls`.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const l = makeLog(); l.refund("a"); l.refund("b"); return l.calls; })()).toEqual(["a", "b"])

items.explanation: The calls array is the recording; the method appends to it so the test can read it afterward.

items.prompt: Implement `makeStore()`: an object with `save(item)` that stores an item and `all()` that returns the items saved so far in order.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const s = makeStore(); s.save("x"); s.save("y"); return s.all(); })()).toEqual(["x", "y"])

items.explanation: This is a tiny fake: it has real state, so later answers depend on earlier calls.

items.prompt: Implement `expiredIds(users, clock)`: return the ids of users whose `trialEndsAt` is before `clock()`, in input order.
items.explanation: The clock is read through the parameter, so the same input always gives the same answer.

items.prompt: Implement `createGatewaySpy()`. It returns an object with a `calls` array and a `refund(chargeId)` method. Each `refund` call appends `{ method: "refund", args: [chargeId] }` to `calls` and returns `{ success: true }`. Each spy starts with its own empty `calls`.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const s = createGatewaySpy(); s.refund("ch_1"); s.refund("ch_2"); return s.calls; })()).toEqual([{ method: "refund", args: ["ch_1"] }, { method: "refund", args: ["ch_2"] }])
expect((() => { const a = createGatewaySpy(); a.refund("x"); return createGatewaySpy().calls.length; })()).toBe(0)

items.explanation: The array is created inside the function, so every spy gets its own. The method records the call and returns what the code under test expects.
items.reference:
Doubles are small
stub clock: a function returning one fixed time
spy: remembers each call's arguments in order
fake: stores what it is given and can return it
the job under test only needs the seam shape
Why: each double is a few lines because it only has to do what the question needs.
items.learnMore:
Building doubles

A double needs only the methods the code under test calls. A spy keeps a list of calls, a fake keeps its stored data, and a stub keeps nothing. Each new double starts empty so tests cannot leak into each other.

Common mistake

Sharing one double between tests, so leftover calls from an earlier test change a later result.
items.reflection: Think of a stand-in you could build in ten minutes for something expensive. What is the least it must do to answer your question?

items.prompt: Implement `createFakeGateway()`. `refund(chargeId)` stores the id and returns `{ success: true, chargeId }`. `getRefunds()` returns the stored ids in the order they were refunded. Each fake starts empty and is independent of other fakes.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const g = createFakeGateway(); g.refund("a"); g.refund("b"); return g.getRefunds(); })()).toEqual(["a", "b"])
expect((() => { const g = createFakeGateway(); g.refund("a"); return createFakeGateway().getRefunds(); })()).toEqual([])

items.explanation: The fake has real state: it stores what it is given and can return it later. The array lives inside the factory, so fakes never share state.

items.prompt: Implement `refundExpiredTrials(users, clock, gateway)`. For each user, in order, whose `trialEndsAt` is less than `clock()` and who has a truthy `pendingChargeId`, call `gateway.refund(user.pendingChargeId)` and collect the user's `id`. Return the collected ids. Use the clock you were given.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const calls = []; const gw = { refund(id) { calls.push(id); } }; return refundExpiredTrials([{ id: "u1", trialEndsAt: 100, pendingChargeId: "ch_1" }, { id: "u2", trialEndsAt: 300, pendingChargeId: "ch_2" }, { id: "u3", trialEndsAt: 50, pendingChargeId: null }], () => 200, gw); })()).toEqual(["u1"])

tests.description: calls the gateway only for the refunded user
tests.expr: expect((() => { const calls = []; const gw = { refund(id) { calls.push(id); } }; refundExpiredTrials([{ id: "u1", trialEndsAt: 100, pendingChargeId: "ch_1" }, { id: "u2", trialEndsAt: 300, pendingChargeId: "ch_2" }, { id: "u3", trialEndsAt: 50, pendingChargeId: null }], () => 200, gw); return calls; })()).toEqual(["ch_1"])

expect((() => { const calls = []; const gw = { refund(id) { calls.push(id); } }; refundExpiredTrials([{ id: "u2", trialEndsAt: 300, pendingChargeId: "ch_2" }], () => 400, gw); return calls; })()).toEqual(["ch_2"])

items.explanation: Both conditions must hold, and the clock is only ever read through the parameter. The gateway double in the tests records which charge ids were requested.
